analysis.one_liner: Requires the EPA to set a national, enforceable limit on PFAS 'forever chemicals' in drinking water.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in September 2019 but never got a full committee markup or a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS are man-made 'forever chemicals' used in firefighting foam, nonstick coatings, and stain repellents that contaminate drinking water supplies, especially near military bases and industrial sites, and may cause adverse health effects. The bill would amend the Safe Drinking Water Act to force the EPA to publish a health goal and issue a national drinking water regulation covering total PFAS within two years. It was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship, received a hearing and a subcommittee vote, and then sat without further action until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and communities whose drinking water is contaminated with PFAS, including residents near military bases, airports, and industrial plants that used the chemicals. The bill would give them an enforceable federal limit on total PFAS in tap water rather than the patchwork of unenforceable health advisories in place.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA must publish a maximum contaminant level goal and issue a national primary drinking water regulation for total PFAS within two years of enactment, giving the chemicals a legally binding limit in drinking water.
The bill amends the Safe Drinking Water Act so the deadline overrides other regulatory timelines, meaning EPA could not let the rule sit indefinitely.
A single national standard covers total PFAS rather than one chemical at a time, addressing the whole class of related compounds found in contaminated water supplies.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers that made or used PFAS, who would face stronger regulation and liability, and water utilities, which would have to install treatment and could pass compliance costs to ratepayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS chemical makers and water utilities

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a hard two-year deadline without funding, so water systems would bear the cost of testing and treatment, and those costs could show up in customers' water bills.

A total-PFAS standard covering the entire chemical class goes beyond EPA's existing chemical-by-chemical approach, which the agency and regulated water systems argued would be very costly to implement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are high: PFAS do not break down in the body or environment and are linked to serious health effects. A national enforceable limit would primarily burden the chemical industry and, to a lesser degree, water systems, whose costs would partly reach customers. A fair bill would have paired the mandate with funding for water systems, but the core trade-off favors public health over industry cost avoidance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee that held a hearing and forwarded it by voice vote in September 2019, but the full committee never marked it up and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Brendan Boyle introduced the bill on April 29, 2019 with bipartisan original cosponsors, including Chairman Frank Pallone (D-NJ) and Republican Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 29, 2019 and to its Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change the next day.
The subcommittee held a hearing on May 15, 2019, and on September 26, 2019 it considered and marked up the bill, forwarding it to the full committee by voice vote.
No further action was taken: the full committee never scheduled a markup, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS manufacturers and other polluters, who avoided a federal two-year deadline for enforceable drinking water limits, while contaminated communities went on waiting for regulation.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but heavily Democratic: 31 of the 32 cosponsors were Democrats, with Representative Fitzpatrick the lone Republican, and no Republican opposition was recorded because the bill never got a vote.

industries.industry: PFAS chemical manufacturers (e.g., makers of firefighting foam and nonstick/stain-resistant chemicals)
industries.note: A national enforceable drinking water limit for total PFAS would tighten regulation of the chemicals and increase cleanup and liability exposure for companies that made them. That exposure is what the public was seeking protection from, so the industry's interest ran against the bill's purpose.

The bill would require utilities to test for and treat total PFAS, a significant cost that would partly fall on ratepayers. Utilities would also benefit from a clear national standard rather than a patchwork of state limits, so the effect cuts both ways.
